Case Vignette: Gerald

Gerald is a 68-year-old married man who has spent the better part of four decades as a school counselor in a mid-sized suburban district. He has always been the kind of man others lean on - steady, warm, the person colleagues seek out in the hallway when something feels too heavy to carry alone. He knows how to sit with other people's pain. What he doesn't know, at least not yet, is how to sit with his own.

Fourteen months ago, Gerald was walking to his car after an evening school board meeting. The parking lot was poorly lit, and he noticed the figure too late. A man approached him from behind a parked van, demanded his wallet, and when Gerald hesitated - not out of defiance, but out of sheer disbelief that this was actually happening - the man struck him twice across the face and shoved him hard against the car door. Gerald fell. He remembers the cold asphalt against his cheek, the sound of footsteps retreating, and the strange, suspended silence that followed. He lay there for what felt like several minutes before a colleague found him.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. The rest has not.

Gerald no longer parks in poorly lit areas. He no longer attends evening events at the school, offering vague excuses about his wife's health or prior commitments. He has rearranged his daily schedule so that he leaves before dusk, something his colleagues have noticed but haven't pressed him on. When he does walk to his car, even in broad daylight, he moves quickly, keys already in hand, eyes sweeping the lot in a way that exhausts him. He tells himself this is simply being sensible. He knows, on some level, it is more than that.

At night, sleep comes reluctantly and leaves early. He wakes at two or three in the morning with his heart already racing, the feeling of the asphalt still vivid against his face, the man's breath still somehow present in the room. His wife, Carol, has learned not to reach for him too suddenly in the dark. The first time she did, he startled so badly he knocked a glass off the nightstand. He apologized for a week.

At work, Gerald moves through his days with a practiced composure that costs him considerably. He sits with students who are struggling - a sophomore whose parents are divorcing, a junior who was bullied online - and he listens with genuine care. But some days, when a student describes feeling cornered or helpless, something shifts inside him. He feels it in his chest first, then a kind of tunneling in his vision, and he has to press his feet flat against the floor beneath his desk and remind himself where he is. He has become quietly hypervigilant about the school's security protocols in ways that feel less professional and more personal.

Gerald has told almost no one what the nights are actually like. He mentioned it once to Carol, minimizing it, framing it as stress. She accepted that because he offered it so calmly, and because Gerald has always seemed capable of managing things. He is aware of the irony - a man who has spent his career teaching young people that asking for help is not weakness, sitting in his own silence and doing the opposite.

What troubles him most is not the fear itself, but the way it has quietly reshaped him. He used to enjoy evening walks. He used to feel at ease in his own neighborhood. He used to be the person who stayed late, who locked up the building, who never thought twice about a dark parking lot. That man feels distant now, almost like someone Gerald used to know. He misses him, and he isn't entirely sure how to find his way back.
